CITY ATTORNEY'S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS

Summary,
Measure — is an amendment to the City Charter proposed by the City Council to update rules

governing public works contracting. Key provisions would: (1) increase the contract threshold
for Council approval from $1,000 to $250,000, (2) retain competitive bidding, but with the ability
to waive certain requirements, and (3) allow the use of alternative procurement mechanisms, for
example “design-build” contracts, when determined by Council to be in the City’s best interests.
These amendments would be implemented through a City Council adopted ordinance.

A "yes" vote on this measure would replace existing City Charter public works rules with the

updated rules summarized above.
A "no" vote on this measure would retain existing Charter public works rules without

amendment.
To pass, the measure requires 50% plus one of votes cast.

Current Charter Provisions
Charter Section 1310 contains current City rules for public works contracting. Key provisions

include:

(1) Council approval required for contracts exceeding $1,000;
(2) Advertisement for bids in an official newspaper required, with waivers allowed only

where Council finds an “urgent necessity;”

(3) All contracts awarded to the lowest responsible bidder;

(4) City employees may construct public works, but only with Council approval for project
values exceeding $1,000.

Per City records, these provisions were originally enacted in 1952 and have not been modified
since.

Proposed Charter Revisions
Measure __ would replace existing Charter rules governing public works with new rules as

follows:

(1) The threshold for Council approval would be increased from $1,000 to $250,000 (“Major
Projects”). The City Manager would approve contracts valued at less than $250,000
(“Minor Projects”).

(2) Competitive bids would still be required for most contracts, with advertisement for bids
and formal bidding required for all “Major Projects;” however, exceptions could be
allowed if justified (e.g., where a limited number of contractors were qualified to perform
required work).

(3) Contracts would continue to be awarded to the lowest responsive/responsible bidder;
however, exceptions would be allowed for “best value” contracting mechanisms, for
example, design-build, where, instead of a separate design contract and a construction
contract awarded to the low bidder, one contract is awarded to a design/construction
team determined to be the most qualified bidder.

(4) The ability for City employees to perform public works would be retained, with City
Council approval required for Major Projects and City Manager Approval for Minor
Projects.

Existing Section 1310 of the City Charter reads as follows: 
 
§ 1310. Contracts on public works. 
 
Every contract involving an expenditure of more than one thousand dollars ($1,000.00) for the 
construction or improvement, (excluding maintenance and repair), of public buildings, works, 
streets, drains, sewers, utilities, parks and playgrounds shall be let to the lowest responsible 
bidder after notice by publication in an official newspaper by one or more insertions, the first of 
which shall be at least ten days before the time for opening bids. 
 
The City Council may reject any and all bids presented and may re-advertise in its discretion.  
 
The City Council, without advertising for bids, or after rejecting bids, or if no bids are received, 
may declare and determine that, in its opinion, the work in question may be performed better or 
more economically by the City with its own employees, and after the adoption of a resolution to 
this effect by at least four affirmative votes, it may proceed to have said work done in the manner 
stated, without further observance of the provisions of this section. Such contracts likewise may 
be let without advertising for bids, if such work shall be deemed by the City Council to be of urgent 
necessity for the preservation of life, health or property, and shall be authorized by motion passed 
by at least four affirmative votes and containing a declaration of the facts constituting such 
urgency. 
 
It is proposed that existing Section 1310 of the City Charter be amended and restated to 
read, in its entirety, as follows: 
 
1310 Public Works 
 
a. 
Rules to be Implemented by Ordinance.  The City Council shall, by ordinance, 
adopt specific policies and procedures for the award of contracts for the construction, 
reconstruction, renovation, alteration, improvement or demolition of public buildings, streets, 
drains, sewers, utilities, parks, playgrounds and similar public facilities (each a “Public Work” and 
collectively, “Public Works”).   
 
b. 
Required Provisions.  The City’s implementing Public Works ordinance 
(“Implementing Ordinance”) shall, at a minimum, contain provisions for the following: 
 
1. 
City Council to retain approval rights over contract awards of $250,000 or greater 
(“Major Projects”), with contract awards of less than $250,000 (“Minor Projects”) 
approved by the City Manager. 
2. 
In general, except as provided below, competitive bid processes for all contracts, 
with formal advertisement for bids and sealed bids required for all Major Projects. 
3. 
In general, except as provided below, the award of contracts to the lowest 
responsive and responsible bidder. 
4. 
The ability to reject any and all bids, to re-advertise for bids, or to waive minor 
defects in any bid if determined by the designated contract-approving authority that 
such action is necessary or appropriate for the benefit of the public; 
5. 
Emergency authority to waive the applicable competitive bid process requirements 
if the approving authority determines that the work required is of urgent necessity 
for the preservation of life, health or property.

6.
The ability of the City to implement Public Works using City employees upon a
determination by the approving authority (the City Council for Major Projects, the
City Manager for Minor Projects) that the work can be performed better or more
economically by City employees;
7.
Defined terms, including definitions for what types of maintenance, repair,
restoration, minor improvements, and equipment installation and equipment
acquisition, which shall not be considered “Public Works” for purposes of this
Section, but shall remain subject to City’s general competitive procurement
standards.
8.
Such other provisions consistent with this Section as may be necessary or
appropriate to implement the City’s Public Works procurement process.
c.
Procurement Alternatives.  The City’s Implementing Ordinance may also provide
for one or more alternative Public Works procurement processes to those described in Subsection 
b, above.  Such alternatives may include, without limitation: (1) sole source or limited bid contracts 
where it is determined by the approving authority that the work required can only be performed 
by one contractor, or a limited group of contractors; (2) “best value” or other alternative 
procurement mechanisms, including but not limited to:  progressive design-build, construction 
manager at risk, fixed-price design-build, and design-build-operate contracts; and/or (3)  such 
other alternative procurement mechanisms or exceptions currently provided under State Law, or 
that may be provided under State Law in the future.  The City’s Implementing Ordinance for any 
such procurement alternatives shall include standards for solicitation, evaluation and selection of 
qualified proponents. No such exception or alternative process shall be applied to a Public Work 
unless it is part of a City-wide policy or program approved by the City Council by ordinance and 
the approving authority has determined that its application to that Public Works is in the best 
overall interests of the City. 
d.
Relationship with Other Laws.  To the maximum extent allowed by law, the
provisions of this Charter Section, and any Implementing Ordinance or policy consistent with the 
terms of this Section, shall supersede all inconsistent State Laws or regulations that may 
otherwise be applicable to the City’s Public Works procurement processes.

approve all settlements of lawsuits and claims greater than $50,000. The California Legislature
set the $50,000 limit in 1989 and has not adjusted it for inflation. Government Code Section 935.4

Council. If a proposed settlement is over the City Manager’s authority, staff will present the case

settlement, or authorize staff to negotiate a settlement up to a certain amount.

authority by ordinance. The City Council could adjust this amount (up or down) in the future by
adopting another ordinance; no further Charter amendment will be necessary. In August 2026,

Manager’s settlement authority at $250,000, the same amount as the City Manager’s current
authority to approve contracts. Any settlement above the Council-set limit in the ordinance

would require City Council approval, and the closed session procedures for City Council approval
of settlements over the amount set by the ordinance would remain the same.

A “YES” vote amends the Charter so that the Council can adopt an ordinance setting the amount

935.4.

Municipal Election in November of the same year.

“councilmembers” since the Council now includes the mayor.

wording of Section 606(c).

to the voters at the next Special Municipal Election consolidated with the next statewide election or

provision that prohibits having more than two appointees on the Council at the same time.

Depending on when a vacancy occurs, this measure could have the effect of lengthening the time
that an appointee serves on the City Council. For example, if the first opportunity for a Special
Municipal Election is the statewide primary in March or June of an even-numbered year, or an earlier
statewide special election, the appointee will serve longer under the proposed amendment than
under the existing Charter provision. At the same time, this measure avoids a situation where the
City must hold a special election to fill a vacancy at the March or June primary followed by a General
Municipal Election in November of the same year.

This measure also re-words Section 606, subsection (c), to refer to the City Council votes rather than
“councilmembers” since the Council now includes the mayor.

A “YES” vote amends the Charter so that a council vacancy filled by appointment goes to voters at
the next November election in an even-numbered year, and makes a clarifying change to the

wording of Section 606(c).
A“NO” vote keeps the existing Charter requirement that a council vacancy filled by appointment go

to the voters at the next Special Municipal Election consolidated with the next statewide election or
the next General Municipal Election, whichever is sooner, and makes no changes to the wording.

This amendment will become effective if a majority of those voting on the measure vote “yes.”
